blocks.text: At the beginning of the 20th century, new experiments and theoretical calculations revealed that classical physics, based on Newton's laws, could not explain phenomena involving extremely small particles or very high velocities. This led to the development of relativistic mechanics, which offered a more comprehensive framework than classical mechanics and fundamentally changed our view of the universe. Albert Einstein's Special Theory of Relativity, introduced in 1905, addressed these issues by proposing that the laws of physics are the same for all observers and that the speed of light is constant, regardless of the observer's motion. The theory not only resolved the conflicts between classical mechanics and electromagnetic theory but also revolutionized our understanding of time, space and motion, forming the basis of what is now known as modern physics.

Consider throwing a ball to your right. For someone facing you, this direction appears to be their left; direction is a relative concept. Similarly, the state of rest or motion of an object depends on the observer. For example, the walls of a moving train seem stationary to passengers inside the train but appear to be moving to someone standing on the ground. Thus we cannot definitively say whether an object is absolutely at rest or in motion; all motions are relative to the observer, or to the frame of reference being used.

This becomes evident from the following example. An observer in a closed train compartment uses the compartment as the frame of reference. To find out about the train's motion, the observer drops a ball and measures the horizontal distance travelled by the ball, keeping the vertical distance the same each time; the vertical distance is covered in t seconds in all cases.

items: Case (a): the train is stationary. The horizontal velocity of the ball is zero and the horizontal distance travelled is also zero. The observations made by the observer inside the train and by someone outside are identical: the ball falls to a point on the floor directly below the point from which it was dropped (Fig. 11.1a).

Case (b): the train moves with a uniform velocity v0. When released, the ball has an initial horizontal velocity v0 and behaves like a projectile, travelling a horizontal distance v0 t in the time t it takes to reach the floor. Since the train and the observer inside it move with the same velocity v0, they travel the same horizontal distance v0 t in the same time. Therefore the observer inside sees the ball fall to a point directly below where it was dropped, while an observer outside sees the ball follow a projectile path (Fig. 11.1b).

blocks.title: Conclusion
blocks.text: Observers in different frames of reference, moving with uniform velocity relative to each other, perceive motion differently. Neither description is wrong; each is correct in its own frame.

Bottom right: the two postulates of special relativity.
blocks.caption: Relative motion, frames of reference and the postulates of special relativity (original diagram after Figure 11.1 and topics 11.1 to 11.3).
blocks.long_description: A ball dropped inside a train moving at steady speed keeps the train's speed, so the passenger sees it fall straight down while someone on the ground sees it trace a projectile curve; motion depends on the frame of reference. In an inertial frame a body at rest stays at rest unless a force acts; an accelerating frame is non-inertial. Special relativity rests on two postulates: the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames, and light in free space has the same speed for every observer. As a result, in a carriage moving at half the speed of light a lamp in the middle reaches both doors together for a passenger, but for someone outside the back door, moving towards the light, opens first.

blocks.prompt: All motions are relative. Is space-time absolute (short question 11.8)? Relativistic mechanics gives results different from classical mechanics for objects moving with what speed (MCQ 11.1)?
blocks.explanation: In special relativity space and time separately are relative: different inertial observers measure different lengths and times. Space-time, which joins them, gives the same interval between two events for every inertial observer, so it is the shared framework; and in Einstein's general theory it is itself curved by mass. Relativistic results differ noticeably from classical ones only for speeds approaching that of light, option (d).

items: Newtonian physics fails for very small particles and very high speeds; Einstein's special theory (1905): the laws of physics are the same for all observers and the speed of light is constant.
Rest and motion are relative. A ball dropped in a uniformly moving train falls straight down for the passenger but follows a projectile path for an outside observer (Fig. 11.1).
